The immediate fantasy impact is volatility: his talent remains obvious, but his reliability is now part of the evaluation. What to watch next is how Kansas City manages his role and whether the trust issue affects usage or availability. [3]

- **Cyrus Allen** — Bleacher Report singled out the rookie as a “WR super-sleeper,” praising his route-running, separation ability, and slot-receiver traits. The Chiefs are looking for juice after losing JuJu Smith-Schuster and another key receiver from last year’s roster, so Allen has a path to compete for a role if his quick-game skill translates. [4]

- **Kenneth Walker III** — Mike Sando’s offseason-move piece says Walker and Dexter Lawrence were acquired this spring to address major needs in Kansas City and Cincinnati, and specifically frames Kansas City’s addition as a much-needed boost to the run game. That matters because it points to a potential scheme and usage shift toward more ground-game support, though the item does not specify Walker’s exact role or acquisition details. [6]

DAL.summary:
- **Christian Parker** — Dallas is entering organized team activities with a first-time defensive coordinator in Parker after last season’s collapse under Matt Eberflus. The Athletic says it may take at least the first month of the season to know whether Parker is truly an upgrade, since preseason and camp evaluation are limited now. That makes early-game sequencing and in-season adjustment the key indicators to watch. [2]

- **Rashan Gary** — The Cowboys are banking on Gary to give the pass rush a real lift after he posted 7.5 sacks in each of the last two seasons. He’s one of the clearest new-impact additions on a defense that badly needs help. His pressure production is central to whether the unit can improve enough to support Parker’s scheme. [2]

- **Brian Schottenheimer, Jerry Jones, Stephen Jones, Will McClay** — Dallas has tried to fix the defense with staff changes and new personnel, but the team has not yet proven the problem is solved. The piece frames the offseason as addressing the issue rather than fully curing it, which raises the bar for the new coaching staff and roster fit. [5]

- **Emmitt Smith** — Smith praised Dallas’ quiet offseason, saying the club does not need “all that drama” and that the focus should be on football. The note specifically points to Brandon Aubrey’s extension and George Pickens’ franchise-tag situation as examples of the offseason calming down. That matters because Dallas is coming off a 7-10 season and needs stability more than headline churn. [8]

SEA.summary:
- **John Schneider** — A 2023 re-draft article argued Seattle’s actual class was stronger than a hypothetical do-over, with Devon Witherspoon and Jaxon Smith-Njigba described as the foundation of the team’s success. The piece also underscored that Schneider targeted elite athletes and landed two top-tier players at their positions. [1]

- **Julian Neal** — Seattle used the No. 99 pick on the Arkansas cornerback after trading down from No. 96 to No. 99 and adding pick No. 216. Neal is described as a physical fit for Mike Macdonald’s defense, but he may need time before he cracks the lineup. [4]

- **Seahawks free agents** — An early look at Seattle’s 2027 free-agent class says the team had a relatively straightforward post-title offseason, with every free agent accounted for before the draft and the majority re-signed. The notable departures listed were Kenneth Walker III, Coby Bryant, Riq Woolen, and Boye Mafe. That points to a future cap-and-attrition watch, especially if those names remain on different timelines by 2027. [7]

DEN.summary:
- **Bo Nix** — Sean Payton has kept the door open for Nix to appear in June OTAs, and The Athletic notes Payton has already said Nix will be full speed throwing by July after two offseason ankle procedures. That keeps his offseason workload worth monitoring, even though his training-camp availability sounds secure. [1, 2]

- **Jaylen Waddle** — Waddle is described as a new speedy target whose arrival pushes everyone else down Denver’s receiver depth chart. In three-receiver sets, Franklin is likely the initial third wideout, while Mims and Bryant are expected to rotate and shuffle into the mix. [1, 2]

- **Justin Joly** — Denver used a fifth-round pick on Joly after trading back into Round 3 for Tyler Onyedim earlier in the draft, and one evaluator called Joly a sleeper who could “change everything.” He enters a crowded tight end room behind Trautman and Engram, but the items make clear he’ll be pushing for snaps immediately. CAR.summary:
- **Bryce Young** — During Carolina’s first OTA session, Young got on his wide receivers and tight ends after several drops in a drill with no defenders, including Xavier Legette. Dave Canales said he loved Young “taking ownership,” and the group responded by cleaning it up for the rest of the rep. It matters because the Panthers want their QB setting the tone for execution, especially with young pass-catchers. [7]

- **Carolina offensive line** — The Panthers’ trench investment is still a major roster-building priority, with Ikem Ekwonu’s fifth-year option exercised and new additions Rasheed Walker and Stone Forsythe now on the books. The cap breakdown underscores how much Carolina has tied up up front, with Ekwonu at $17.5 million, Walker at $4 million, and Forsythe at $2 million; the exact cap percentage isn’t specified. That signals the line remains central to Bryce Young’s support system and to how the roster is constructed. [8]

NO.summary:
- **Herron (OL)** — The Saints are a team to watch for undrafted free-agent offensive linemen, and Herron is highlighted as the top one to monitor during OTAs. He started all 24 games at right tackle for Maryland and is described as a strong fit because New Orleans lacks O-line depth. That gives him a real shot at at least the practice squad, with near-term roster value if the line gets hit by injuries. [1]

- **Zxavian Harris** — The Saints added Harris as a UDFA defensive tackle, and the note frames him as a player with “Day 2 talent” despite off-field issues and a recent right-foot surgery. He produced 123 tackles, 17.5 TFLs and 5.5 sacks at Ole Miss, and New Orleans’ draft investment at the position does not necessarily close the door on him. He could still push for a near-term roster spot or depth role if he shows he’s healthy. [1]

- **Donaldson (RB)** — Donaldson is being tracked as a potential surprise at running back, where the Saints need a dependable backup and short-yardage option. He scored 34 touchdowns over the last three seasons, including 11 at Ohio State, and the report specifically points to his downhill style and contact balance as traits New Orleans lacks. His OTAs performance will matter for a roster that still has a clear depth need behind the top backs. [1]

- **Saints offense / depth chart** — New Orleans enters OTAs with unresolved depth questions at running back, wide receiver and especially along the offensive line, with center depth behind Erik McCoy called out as a concern. That makes the spring practices meaningful for fringe players trying to carve out roles. It also raises the importance of the incoming rookie/UDFA group because depth is not specified as settled anywhere else. [8]

NYJ.summary:
- **Stephens** — OTAs give him a chance to reset his Jets narrative after an uneven first season in New York. The piece notes he was signed to a three-year, $36 million deal, and he finished last year with 73 tackles, one forced fumble, nine passes defended, and four stuffs. That production shows a useful floor, but the next step is turning more of those plays into interceptions and more consistent impact. [7]

- **Brady Cook** — His path to the QB2 job has improved because the Jets still have not added a veteran backup such as Russell Wilson or Cooper Rush. With OTAs starting, Cook can compete for both the backup role and possibly QB3, while the team appears willing to let the current quarterbacks “fight it out.” That keeps the depth chart unsettled behind Geno Smith and makes Cook a name to monitor in camp. - **Caleb Williams** — The Bears are finally getting Williams into live OTA work against the defense after weeks of drills and routes on air. It’s still non-contact, but this is the first real look at how he operates in Ben Johnson’s offense once the defense is involved. [1]

That signals a roster-wide pressure point, especially for depth-chart battles and role players trying to lock down snaps. [1]

- **Colston Loveland** — Loveland’s role as the Bears’ TE1 is “not up for debate,” according to the item. The bigger question is whether he settles in as merely a good starter or pushes toward top-tier fantasy relevance at tight end. [8]

ATL.summary:
- **Riley Mahlman** — The Falcons signed the massive undrafted tackle as one of three UDFA linemen, and Bleacher Report labeled him Atlanta’s “most exciting” undrafted free agent. He’s viewed as a potential swing tackle because of his length and experience on both sides, though his below-average play strength and shorter arms raise questions about a possible move inside. That makes him a developmental depth piece whose best path to a roster spot is likely tied to coaching up and added NFL strength. [1]

- **James Brockermeyer** — Atlanta added the center as another undrafted lineman, and he drew notice for his Senior Bowl pass-protection work and quick feet. The Falcons reportedly have only two other centers on the offseason roster, so his path may be cleaner than Mahlman’s. He looks like a legitimate summer roster contender if that interior-line depth chart stays thin. [1]

- **Jack Strand** — The Falcons brought in the Division II quarterback as one of three new signal-callers at offseason workouts. The preseason will be the real test, with Strand in the mix to challenge veteran Trevor Siemian for the QB3 job. His college production was big, but the roster battle is the relevant part here. [1]

- **Michael Penix Jr.** — NFL Network tagged the Falcons quarterback as a “make or break” player entering a season where he has to solidify the starting job. The key context is the new front office and coaching staff did not draft him, so his play matters not just for Atlanta’s offense but for how the organization evaluates its long-term quarterback plan. [6]

- **Falcons offense personnel groupings** — Atlanta’s offseason additions point toward heavier use of 12 personnel and some 21 personnel looks. The team drafted Zachariah Branch, signed Austin Hooper, already has Kyle Pitts and Charlie Woerner, and added Brian Robinson, which suggests a more multiple offense than a pure three-wide setup. That could create interesting fantasy usage splits for the pass catchers and backs if those grouping tendencies carry over. [4]

BAL.summary:
- **Jaylinn Hawkins** — The Ravens added Hawkins on a two-year, $10 million deal after he drew interest from Houston and Carolina, and he said Baltimore sold him on the culture and its vision for his role under the new staff. That makes him an underrated offseason addition in a secondary that values versatility, and his fit should be easier to see once camp roles are sorted. [6]

- **Josh Cuevas** — Baltimore’s fifth-round tight end is being framed as a candidate to help replace some of Isaiah Likely’s pass-catching, slot-usage, and playmaking workload. If Cuevas can carve out that complementary receiving role, he has a real path to immediate fantasy relevance in a TE room that just lost production. [8]

- **Declan Doyle and Joe Lombardi** — The Ravens paired rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle, who has never called plays, with Joe Lombardi as senior offensive assistant despite Lombardi’s checkered history as a coordinator. That combination puts extra pressure on the offensive staff to maximize Lamar Jackson’s production, and it raises questions about how stable the scheme will be early. [7]

IND.summary:
- **Josh Downs** — The piece says Downs is set to remain the Colts’ starting slot receiver, but he’s positioned for a bigger role because Michael Pittman Jr. is now in Pittsburgh and there’s an opening at outside receiver. Downs had a brief production dip last year with Alec Pierce and rookie Tyler Warren absorbing targets, so this setup points to a likely rebound in both snaps and target share. [2]

- **Laiatu Latu** — Latu heads into OTAs as the centerpiece of the Colts’ pass-rush plans after posting 8.5 sacks in his second season, up from 4 as a rookie. The team is counting on him to deliver his first double-digit sack season, which would be a major boost for a defense that has turned over much of its edge rotation. [4]

- **Jaylahn Tuimoloau** — Tuimoloau is slated to start opposite Latu in year two, though the report notes he still has to earn the role. His physical development has been a focus since his rookie season ended, so OTAs are an early audition for a key edge spot and a chance to lock down a larger snap share. [4]

JAX.summary:
- **Nate Boerkircher** — The Jaguars’ top pick in the 2026 draft looked comfortable in his first OTA session, showing strong hands in blocking drills and catching an over-the-middle pass for a solid gain. He is behind Brenton Strange on the tight end depth chart, but the early usage suggests Boerkircher could carve out a meaningful role once pads come on. [1]

- **Emmanuel Pregnon** — The rookie offensive lineman stood out physically at OTA No. 1 and looked like one of the most imposing bodies on the line. His path to guard snaps is crowded, though, with Ezra Cleveland, Patrick Mekari and Wyatt Milum all set to factor into the competition. [1]

- **Tanner Koziol** — Koziol had a quiet practice, largely because the Jaguars’ tight end room is already busy with Brenton Strange, Nate Boerkircher and Quintin Morris getting attention. He is going to have to fight for reps, but the fit with tight ends coach Richard Angulo looks promising, especially in run blocking. [1]

- **Jalen Huskey** — The Jaguars used Huskey in a variety of ways in his first look with the veteran roster, even though he did not record a pass breakup or interception. Safety appears deep, with Caleb Ransaw back, Antonio Johnson active and Eric Murray picking off Trevor Lawrence, so Huskey’s route to playing time looks competitive. [1]

- **Tank Bigsby** — Bigsby’s departure to Philadelphia is tied directly to being displaced in the running back pecking order by Jaguars rookie Bhayshul Tuten. That points to Tuten having already altered the backfield hierarchy in Jacksonville before the season even began. [2]

PHI.summary:
- **Tank Bigsby (RB)** — NFL.com’s NFC underappreciated-player piece singled him out as a reminder that he exists in Philadelphia after last September’s trade from Jacksonville. The note emphasized that he flashed efficiency — 5.9 yards per carry and 13 explosive runs — even if his 104-yard game was overshadowed by Saquon Barkley’s production. That keeps Bigsby on the radar as a depth back whose role is worth monitoring if the Eagles keep searching for efficiency behind Barkley. [1]

- **Jalen Hurts** — The Athletic says Hurts is in a pivotal year, with a contract extension potentially looming after this season, and that OTAs are the start of his transition into a new, more open offense. How smoothly he adapts is the key storyline to watch through minicamp and summer work. If the offense opens up as intended, it matters for both his fantasy ceiling and the Eagles’ long-term commitment decisions. [3]

- **A.J. Brown** — The Eagles’ trade chatter around Brown is still active in today’s coverage, with SI Eagles framing a move as likely and suggesting Howie Roseman should continue taking offers through the spring. The timing angle centers on June 1 and the rest of minicamp. If the Eagles seriously entertain a deal, it would reshape the passing game immediately and create a major target-share vacuum. [7]
